newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Jospin wants flexibility on deficit target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jospin wants flexibility on deficit target.

text.p: French Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin said on Monday that if his party won the current parliamentary election it would put conditions on France's entry into the European single currency.

In an interview with Europe 1 radio, Jospin said that he wanted a flexible view of the need to cut the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), preferring to look at the criterion as a "trend" instead of a fixed figure.
Jospin insisted that the southern European countries, notably Italy, should join the single currency from the start.
"I do not want to dissolve France into Europe, " Jospin told Europe 1 radio.

"I want a France that has weight in Europe and a Europe that chooses economic growth and employment, that stops restraining the economic machinery at the time that the United States, Latin America, Japan (and) Asia, advance with big steps. That is the choice for the French people," Jospin said.
"If we continue with Europe in the way it is shaping up at the moment, including the monetary aspects, we will gradually kill the European spirit of the people," he added.

Former French prime minister Edouard Balladur also called for a flexible interpretation of the criteria for a single European currency and said major countries such as Italy and Spain should join from the start if possible.

"I want these criteria to be interpreted with a bit of flexibility," said Balladur on television on Sunday night. Balladur was conservative prime minister from 1993 to 1995 and is campaigning for the centre-right coalition in the race for May 25-June 1 parliamentary elections.
Jospin was the Socialist candidate in the presidential election of May 1995 won by conservative Jacques Chirac.
While Socialist president Francois Mitterand was one of the enthusiasts for European Monetary Union, Jospin said France needed to put conditions on its entry.

"We should not enter the single currency without conditions ...If we do not put in place an economic government to counterbalance the (European) central bank charged with managing the European currency... that would mean that we would give up our monetary policy," he said.

"And if we accept the re-inforced stability pact, which was not in the Maastricht Treaty and which the Germans imposed on us, that would mean we would give up our budgetary policy as well," Jospin said. "That is to say the two principle instruments of economic policy," he said.

Jospin said the Socialist party would not re-nationalise privatised companies. But he said that his party would not continue the sale of telecommunications operator France Telecom, the Thomson electronics group, Air France or the EDF/GDF electricity and gas utilities.

The centre-right government has postponed the sale of a 30 to 35 percent stake in France Telecom by four weeks as the marketing of the biggest French market flotation ever clashed with the election campaign.

The latest opinion poll in France's parliamentary election campaign, published on Monday, gave the centre-right coalition a narrow majority and found more than one-third of voters could change their minds.

The BVA poll for France 2 television and Europe 1 radio said that if the election were held now, the ruling RPR-UDF coalition would win 296 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France, Socialists 238, Communists 18, ecologists two and the extreme-right National Front one.
